items: Tomorrow
Your coordinator has ten minutes and has read neither document. She has to answer a parent this afternoon.
What she needs
What the course promises, what the plan actually does, and where the two do not line up.
The trap
If you say it without saying where it came from, she cannot use it. She has to quote something to a parent.

predicao.prompt: Two documents about the same course, written four months apart. Where do they usually stop agreeing first?
choices: In the topics — the plan covers different subjects
In the time — the plan needs more hours than the course has
In the level — the plan is written for a different level
predicao.why: B. Topics are what everyone checks, so they rarely drift. Time is what nobody recounts after the first version — and it is what breaks first, because every good activity takes longer than it looks on paper. If you chose C, you were thinking about a bigger failure than the usual one.

texto.rtitle: Document A -- Course syllabus, published to families in February
paras: Intermediate Conversation, 30 hours. Each session runs for 90 minutes and covers one unit of the coursebook. Students complete the book in twenty sessions.
Every session ends with a short writing task, collected and returned with written feedback the following week. Speaking is assessed twice: once at session ten and once at the end.
The course assumes no work outside the classroom.

texto.rtitle: Document B -- Lesson plan for Unit 7, written in June
paras: Unit 7 -- Making Complaints. 90 minutes. Lead-in 10, vocabulary 15, listening 20, controlled practice 15, role-play 25, feedback 10.
Homework: students write the complaint email at home and bring it printed. The email is corrected in pairs at the start of the following session, not by the teacher.
Note for whoever teaches this: the role-play needs the full 25 minutes. If the listening runs over, cut the controlled practice, never the role-play.

gist_texto.prompt: Read both once. What is the overall relationship between them?
choices: The plan follows the syllabus closely
The plan is a different course from the one the syllabus promised
The plan is the same course, but it quietly changed three of the promises
gist_texto.why: C. The unit, the level and the 90 minutes all match — this is not a different course. But three promises moved: the total time, who corrects the writing, and whether there is homework. B overstates it and A misses it, which is exactly the pair of mistakes a coordinator cannot afford in front of a parent.

detalhe_evi.title: Three things that stopped lining up. Each one with the line that shows it.
items: The plan needs more minutes than the session has.
B: 10+15+20+15+25+10 = 95, and B itself says 90. A says 90.
The writing is no longer corrected by the teacher.
A: 'collected and returned with written feedback'. B: 'corrected in pairs at the start of the following session, not by the teacher'.
There is homework now.
A: 'assumes no work outside the classroom'. B: 'students write the complaint email at home'.
The plan covers a different unit from the one the syllabus describes.
f
Both are Unit 7 of the same book, 90 minutes. The course did not change — three promises inside it did.
The plan says which activity to cut if time runs out.
t
B, note at the end: 'if the listening runs over, cut the controlled practice, never the role-play'.
The syllabus promises two speaking assessments.
t
A: 'once at session ten and once at the end'. The plan says nothing about assessment — which is a silence, not a disagreement.

disc_sort.title: Six statements about the two documents. Sort each by what it is.
cols: In the text — you can quote it
Between the texts — you had to compare
Yours — the text does not say it
items: The plan allocates 95 minutes to a 90-minute session.
The plan gives the writing to the students to correct.
The plan needs five minutes it does not have.
The two documents disagree about homework.
Whoever wrote the plan had not reread the syllabus.
The role-play matters more to the writer than the controlled practice.

disc_reveal.title: Why the third column is the dangerous one
disc_reveal.sub: Read each, decide whether you would say it to the coordinator, then click.
items: “Whoever wrote the plan had not reread the syllabus.”
Probably true, and unusable: no line says it. If she repeats it to a parent she is repeating YOUR guess with the school's authority behind it.
essencial
“The role-play matters more to the writer than the controlled practice.”
This one is nearly quotable — the note says cut the practice, never the role-play. Say it that way and it moves to column one.
essencial
“The plan needs five minutes it does not have.”
Column two: neither document says it. You got it by adding six numbers — and adding is fine, as long as you say you added.
condicional

disc_answer.title: Reveal the rule you are actually using
list: QUOTE it — the line exists. 'The plan gives the writing to the students.'
DERIVE it — you compared or counted. Say so: 'Adding up the plan, it comes to 95.'
OWN it — no line supports it. Say it is yours: 'My reading is that…' — or do not say it.
The coordinator can defend the first two in front of a parent. The third she can only defend as YOUR opinion, so she has to know it is one.
disc_answer.note: This is the whole lesson. The English for it is on the next screen.

prep_phrases.title: Three ways to say where it came from
items: The syllabus says the writing comes back corrected.
quote — the line exists
The syllabus says the writing comes back corrected.
Putting the two together, the plan needs five minutes it does not have.
derive — you compared
Putting the two together, the plan needs five minutes it does not have.
My reading is that nobody reread the syllabus in June.
own it — no line says this
My reading is that nobody reread the syllabus in June.
The plan says X, but the syllabus has Y.
naming the divergence
The plan says X, but the syllabus has Y.
These two do not line up on who corrects the writing.
naming it the other way
These two do not line up on who corrects the writing.

prep_reph.title: Say each one again, with the source attached.
items: They took the homework rule out.
The plan says… / the syllabus says…
The plan does not fit in the session.
Putting the two together…
They stopped caring about the writing.
My reading is that… — or cut it
Your side
Three minutes for the coordinator. What the course promises, what the plan does, the three divergences — and where each one comes from.
Her side
Your teacher is the coordinator. She will interrupt twice: once to ask where something came from, and once to repeat one of your points back WRONG.

task_brief.label: Take these in. Keywords, not sentences.
items: the syllabus says
the plan says
putting the two together
my reading is that
let me check that in the plan

task_brief.label: Three minutes. That is what she has.

wb.title: How it went
campos: Anything said as fact that was actually hers (for the checkpoint)

retask.title: Say only the point your teacher marked — once more.
items: Same content. What changes is whether she could quote you to a parent.

fecho.title: What we built today
items: Quote it when the line exists — she can read it out loud.
Say you derived it when you compared or counted. Adding is fine; hiding that you added is not.
Own it when no line supports it, or leave it out.
A divergence is only useful if she can say where each half came from.

fecho.title: How confident do you feel right now?
fecho.sub: Your own reading, today. There is no right answer here.
